title: Turning points of US history
description: Independence (1776), the Constitution (1787), the Civil War (1861 to 1865) and the end of slavery (1865), Pearl Harbor (1941) and the Moon landing (1969).

facts.text: Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, brought the United States into World War II.

title: The Dawes Act and allotment
description: Allotment split reservations into individual plots and sold the rest, cutting Native land by about two-thirds.

facts.text: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended allotment.

title: Chinese exclusion and Angel Island
description: The 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act singled out one nationality; Angel Island held Asian immigrants for weeks or months.

facts.text: Congress repealed the Chinese exclusion laws in 1943, when China was a World War II ally.

title: Winning the 19th Amendment
description: Catt’s Winning Plan and Paul’s pickets pushed the 19th Amendment to ratification in August 1920.

facts.text: On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, after Harry Burn cast the deciding vote.

title: An urban nation
description: By 1920, rails, factories and immigration had made the US a nation where most people lived in urban areas.

facts.text: The 1920 census was the first in which most Americans lived in urban areas.

title: The war with Spain
description: How the 1898 war over Cuba left the US with colonies in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

facts.text: From 1895 to 1898 Cuban revolutionaries fought for independence from Spain, and many Americans sympathized with them.
The US battleship Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor on February 15, 1898.
The US declared war on Spain on April 25, 1898, and in the Teller Amendment Congress pledged not to annex Cuba.
In the Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, Spain ceded Puerto Rico and Guam and sold the Philippines to the US for $20 million.
In 1893 planters and businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Hawaii's Queen Liliuokalani; the US annexed Hawaii in 1898.
In 1897 more than 21,000 Native Hawaiians signed petitions against annexation, and the annexation treaty failed in the Senate.

title: Empire debated
description: How Filipinos fought for independence and how imperialists and anti-imperialists argued over annexation.

facts.text: Filipino revolutionaries led by Emilio Aguinaldo proclaimed an independent Philippine Republic; they wanted independence, not new rulers.
The Philippine-American War (1899 to 1902) killed over 4,200 US and over 20,000 Filipino soldiers; up to 200,000 Filipino civilians died.
Annexation backers wanted Asian trade, doubted Filipinos could govern themselves, and feared Germany or Japan would take the islands.
The Anti-Imperialist League, formed in 1898 to fight annexing the Philippines, included Andrew Carnegie, Mark Twain and Samuel Gompers.
The league's 1899 platform declared that "governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed."

title: From neutrality to war
description: How submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram moved the US from neutrality to war in 1917.

facts.text: When war broke out in Europe in 1914, Wilson declared the US neutral; he was reelected in 1916 on the slogan "He kept us out of war."
A German submarine sank the British liner Lusitania on May 7, 1915, killing 128 Americans; Wilson still kept the US out of the war.
On February 1, 1917, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, attacking Allied and neutral ships in war zones.
The Zimmermann Telegram proposed that Mexico ally with Germany and "reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona."
Wilson asked Congress for war on April 2, 1917, and Congress declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917.

title: Arguing over war
description: What Wilson and his opponents in Congress argued about joining World War I.

facts.text: In his war message, Wilson declared: "The world must be made safe for democracy."
By 1917 American bankers had loaned the Allies over $2 billion.
House opponents argued no vital interest was threatened, the public didn't want war, and arms makers and business interests were pushing it.
The House voted 373 to 50 for war; Jeannette Rankin, the first woman in Congress, told the House: "I cannot vote for war."

title: Americans in the fight
description: How American troops, including Black and Native soldiers, fought in France in 1918.

facts.text: The Meuse-Argonne Offensive, from September 26 to November 11, 1918, was the AEF's largest operation, with over a million US soldiers.
The fighting ended with an armistice on November 11, 1918.
The 369th Infantry, a Black regiment called the Harlem Hellfighters, spent 191 days in front-line trenches, more than any US unit its size.
In France in 1918, Choctaw soldiers became the first Code Talkers, sending battle messages in Choctaw that the enemy never broke.

title: The Great Migration
description: Why millions of Black Southerners moved north and west, and what they found there.

facts.text: From the 1910s to the 1970s, about six million Black Southerners moved north and west, one of the largest migrations in US history.
Migrants left to escape racial violence and the oppression of Jim Crow, and to find better jobs and schooling.
From 1917, men leaving for the war and a drop in immigration from Europe opened industrial jobs to Black workers.
Migrants settled in cities such as New York, Chicago and Detroit.
In the North, migrants still met discrimination, including in housing, and racial violence in the Red Summer of 1919.

title: The Harlem Renaissance
description: How Black writers and musicians in Harlem, such as Langston Hughes, celebrated African American culture.

facts.text: Langston Hughes, whose first book of poems, The Weary Blues, appeared in 1926, became a leading writer of the Harlem Renaissance.
The Harlem Renaissance celebrated African American culture and achievement.
Hughes said the people he met in everyday life inspired his work, and blues and jazz gave it its rhythm.

title: Prohibition
description: Why temperance reformers won a national ban on alcohol, and what the ban produced.

facts.text: From the 1870s the Women's Christian Temperance Union saw alcohol as the source of many social ills, including ruined families.
The 18th Amendment banned the "manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors" for beverage purposes.
National Prohibition began in January 1920.
Illegal liquor stayed easy to find, and gangsters like Al Capone grew rich from bootlegging while bribing police, judges and politicians.

title: Repeal
description: Why Americans, led in part by women's groups, repealed Prohibition in 1933.

facts.text: In 1929 Pauline Sabin founded the Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform, which grew to 1.5 million reported members.
Repeal women argued Prohibition had led to more unregulated and underage drinking and to distrust of the law.
After the 1929 crash, the promise of jobs and tax revenue from legal alcohol built support for repeal.
The 21st Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the 18th Amendment and ended national Prohibition.

title: Living through the Depression
description: How ordinary Americans lived through the crash, joblessness and forced removals of the 1930s.

facts.text: On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, the stock market fell nearly 12 percent; by mid-November it had lost almost half its value.
At the Depression's worst, in 1933, about a quarter of the workforce (24.9 percent) had no job.
Homeless families built shantytowns from packing crates and scrap, nicknamed "Hoovervilles."
In the 1930s officials pushed Mexicans and Mexican Americans, many US-born citizens, to Mexico; estimates range from 400,000 to 2 million.

title: The Dust Bowl
description: Why drought and farming practices turned the southern Plains into the Dust Bowl and drove families west.

facts.text: Repeated droughts struck Plains farms that had spread onto poorer land and cut back on soil conservation, leaving soil to blow away.
On Black Sunday, April 14, 1935, a wall of dust turned a sunny afternoon darker than night across the southern Plains.
An Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, coined the term Dust Bowl in 1935.
Many Plains families, called "Okies," abandoned their farms and headed to California in search of work.

title: The New Deal's programs
description: What the New Deal built, from the CCC to Social Security.

facts.text: In his first inaugural address, on March 4, 1933, FDR said "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself."
New Deal agencies such as the CCC (1933) and the WPA put unemployed Americans to work on conservation, construction and arts projects.
By 1942, over 2.5 million men had served in the Civilian Conservation Corps.
The Social Security Act, signed August 14, 1935, created old-age benefits and unemployment insurance.

title: Who the New Deal left out
description: How Social Security's exclusions left out most Black workers, and how historians explain them.

facts.text: The act left out agricultural workers and domestic servants in private homes.
About 65 percent of African Americans were left out of the new benefits.
In 1935 the NAACP's Charles Hamilton Houston warned Congress the exemptions would leave out Black sharecroppers and tenants.
Social Security historian Larry DeWitt argues the exclusions came from the practical problem of collecting taxes, not racial motives.

title: Critics left and right
description: Why some critics said the New Deal went too far and others said it did not go far enough.

facts.text: Senator Huey Long pushed his Share Our Wealth plan to spread wealth; by spring 1935 over seven million Americans had joined its societies.
The American Liberty League, founded in 1934 by business leaders and politicians, attacked the New Deal as unconstitutional.

title: Staying out
description: Why Congress passed Neutrality Acts in the 1930s.

facts.text: In the 1930s, Senator Gerald Nye's report claimed bankers and arms makers had pushed the US into World War I for their own profit.
The first Neutrality Act, passed August 31, 1935, banned exporting "arms, ammunition, and implements of war" to nations at war.

title: Aiding Britain
description: How the US moved from cash and carry to Lend-Lease, and who opposed it.

facts.text: In November 1939 a new Neutrality Act let nations at war buy arms from the US on a "cash and carry" basis.
In 1940 FDR won a third term, breaking the two-term tradition set by George Washington.
Under Lend-Lease, passed in March 1941, the US supplied Britain with war materials without demanding immediate payment.
Many Americans opposed another war, and Army chief George Marshall argued supplies should be saved to defend the Western Hemisphere.

title: Why Japan attacked
description: How the US embargo on Japan led to the attack on Pearl Harbor and war on two fronts.

facts.text: As Japan pushed into China and Indochina, the US froze Japanese assets and imposed a full embargo on exports to Japan, including oil.
The attack on Pearl Harbor killed more than 2,400 Americans.
The day after the attack the US declared war on Japan; when Germany then declared war on the US, it faced war in Europe and Asia.

title: Winning the war
description: How the US fought on two fronts, from Midway and D-Day to Japan's surrender.

facts.text: At Midway, June 4 to 7, 1942, US code breakers uncovered Japan's plan and Japan lost four aircraft carriers, turning the Pacific war.
On D-Day, June 6, 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed in Normandy, France; Americans came ashore at Utah and Omaha beaches.
Germany surrendered in May 1945.
Japan formally surrendered aboard USS Missouri on September 2, 1945, ending World War II.
The Marines trained over 400 Navajo men as Code Talkers, many serving in the Pacific, and the Japanese never broke their code.
The US military grew from about 334,000 people in 1939 to over 12 million in 1945.

title: The atomic bomb debate
description: What happened at Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and how historians disagree about the decision.

facts.text: The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on August 6 and Nagasaki on August 9, 1945; the next day Japan's emperor pushed to surrender.
Historians called traditionalists argue the bombs were necessary to save American lives and prevent a US invasion of Japan.
Revisionists such as Gar Alperovitz argue the bombs were unnecessary since Japan was near surrender, and partly aimed at the Soviets.

title: New work, new demands
description: How the war opened jobs to women and how Black Americans pressed for equal treatment.

facts.text: More than six million women took wartime factory jobs; Rosie the Riveter became their symbol.
Labor leader A. Philip Randolph threatened to bring tens of thousands of Black marchers to Washington unless defense jobs opened to them.
Executive Order 8802, issued June 25, 1941, declared "There shall be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries."
In 1942 the Pittsburgh Courier, a Black newspaper, launched the Double V campaign: victory over fascism abroad and racism at home.

title: Japanese American incarceration
description: Why Japanese Americans were forced into camps, and how the country later apologized.

facts.text: Executive Order 9066, issued February 19, 1942, led to the forced removal of about 122,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
Nearly 70,000 of them were US citizens; none were charged with a crime, and they had no way to appeal.
The government called the guarded camps "relocation centers"; they were also known as "internment camps."
Gordon Hirabayashi and Fred Korematsu challenged the orders in court, but the Supreme Court upheld them.
More than 30,000 Japanese Americans served in World War II, in segregated units.
In 1988 Congress apologized for the incarceration and paid $20,000 to each person who had been held.

title: A world power with a bigger government
description: How war, boom and depression between 1898 and 1945 made the US a world power with a much larger federal government.

facts.text: Before the Great Depression, federal spending was less than 3 percent of GDP; by 1939 federal outlays exceeded 10 percent.
